name: When Students May Use AI in Science
title: When Students May Use AI in Science
answer: This idea is that science and computer science teachers need task-specific rules for when students may use AI, just as math teachers do. The rules should match the learning goal of each task, and students should disclose which AI tool they used and for what. This matters because it keeps AI use honest, visible, and aligned with what students are supposed to learn.

sections.body: Science and computer science classrooms need clear boundaries for student AI use, because a single blanket rule does not fit every assignment. The book points to the AI use levels from Chapter 3 as a workable structure for setting those boundaries. A lab report, a research project, and a coding exercise can each carry different permissions depending on what the task is meant to teach. The problem this solves is confusion about whether AI is helping students learn or replacing the skill they are supposed to practice. By tying permission to purpose, teachers can make AI use predictable and defensible.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher sets the AI rule for each task by asking what the task is meant to develop. For a lab report, the rule might permit AI feedback on a draft while forbidding AI writing. For a research project on a science topic, AI might be allowed to help find sources, but students must then check those sources themselves. For a coding exercise that builds basic skills, the task might be marked no AI at all. The text gives no grade bands, so the same logic applies wherever the task appears: when the goal is designing an experiment, AI should act as a coach rather than the designer; when the goal is debugging code, AI should explain errors rather than repair them; and when the goal is exploring a big data set, AI might help with analysis so students can focus on what the results mean.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It presents the approach as a practical extension of the AI use levels from Chapter 3 and as a way to match rules to task purpose. Because no research finding is cited, this idea rests on practice rather than research. The book's guidance is that the levels work well for science and computer science, but that is a claim from practice, not a cited study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits come from the purpose of the task. AI should not take over the design of an experiment when the goal is learning to design one, and it should not repair code when the goal is learning to debug. AI may help with analysis of a big data set, but the students still need to focus on what the results mean. Students should disclose how they used AI, with a short note at the end of a lab report or project saying which tool was used and for what. Teachers remain the ones who set and adjust the rules, using those notes to see how students are using tools and to change the rules over time.
